Roman Pasta and Chickpeas

A Roman chickpea-and-pasta soup scented with rosemary and enriched with anchovies and tomato.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

1 1/2 cups dried chickpeas
1 1/2 cups cannolicchi or maltagliati pasta
1 garlic clove
4 oil-packed anchovy fillets
2 tbsp tomato sauce
1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil
2 rosemary sprigs
1 1/3 tsp fine salt
1/2 tsp ground black pepper
6 1/3 cups warm water for soaking
8 1/2 cups fresh water for cooking the chickpeas

Preparation

1. Put the chickpeas in a bowl with the warm soaking water and soak for 12 hours.

2. Drain and rinse the chickpeas.

3. Transfer them to a pot with the fresh cooking water and rosemary.

4. Bring to a gentle boil and cook over low heat for 2 hours, until tender but still intact.

5. Remove the rosemary. Measure and reserve 3 cups of chickpea cooking water.

6. Heat 3 tablespoons olive oil in a skillet. Add the whole garlic clove and cook for 2 minutes.

7. Add the anchovy fillets and mash them with a fork until dissolved into the oil.

8. Remove the garlic. Add the tomato sauce and cook over high heat for 3 minutes.

9. Pour the mixture into the pot with the chickpeas.

10. Add 2 cups reserved chickpea cooking water and 1 teaspoon salt. Simmer for 10 minutes.

11. Bring to a boil and add the pasta.

12. Cook for about 8 minutes, stirring regularly. Add the remaining 1 cup reserved chickpea water during cooking.

13. Turn off the heat and stir in the remaining 1 tablespoon olive oil, remaining 1/3 teaspoon salt, and black pepper.

14. Rest for 3 minutes.

Serving

Divide among 4 bowls and serve hot.

Chef's Note

The anchovies should dissolve completely into the oil, adding savory depth without leaving an overt fish flavor. The final rest allows the pasta starch to thicken the soup naturally.
t: Roman pasta and chickpeas has been documented for well over a century. The Roman hallmark is the addition of anchovy to the chickpea base, along with rosemary, creating a deeply savory variation on Italy’s widespread tradition of combining pasta and legumes.
u: Tender chickpeas and small pasta simmer together in a rosemary-scented broth deepened with anchovy, garlic, and tomato. Creamy from natural starch rather than dairy, it is rustic, savory, warming, and substantial enough to stand alone as a meal.
v:
Add a small squeeze of lemon at the end — brightens the savory fish note and keeps the overall flavor from feeling too heavy.
Add a small acidic finish such as lemon juice or wine vinegar — sharpens earthy legume flavors and makes the dish taste fresher.
Finish with fresh basil or parsley — adds a fresh aromatic note that lifts the cooked tomato flavor without changing the core sauce.

Roman Pasta and Broccoli

A Roman soup of broken spaghetti and Romanesco broccoli with anchovy, aromatic vegetables, tomato, and chile.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

2/3 lb spaghetti, broken into short lengths
1 Romanesco broccoli, about 1 3/4 lb
4 1/4 cups vegetable broth
2 garlic cloves
2 anchovy fillets
1/2 carrot
1/2 celery stalk
1/2 onion
2 tsp tomato paste
1 small red chile
1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil
3/4 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Keep the vegetable broth hot at a gentle simmer.

2. Clean the broccoli, remove the outer leaves, and divide the head into florets. Cut the tender stems into 3/4-inch pieces.

3. Finely chop the carrot, celery, and onion.

4. Heat the olive oil in a large pot.

5. Add the crushed garlic, anchovy fillets, and halved chile. Cook for 1 minute.

6. Add the carrot, celery, and onion and cook over medium heat for 5 minutes.

7. Dissolve the tomato paste in 1/4 cup hot broth and pour it into the pot.

8. Add the broccoli florets and stems and cook for 10 minutes, stirring every 2 minutes.

9. Add the remaining 4 cups broth, cover, and cook over low heat for 10 minutes.

10. Remove about 2 cups intact florets and set aside.

11. Blend the soup for 20–30 seconds with an immersion blender, keeping a slightly rustic texture.

12. Return the whole florets to the pot and bring back to a boil.

13. Add the salt and broken spaghetti.

14. Cook the pasta directly in the soup for the package cooking time, stirring often.

Serving

Divide among 4 bowls and serve very hot.

Chef's Note

Reserve some whole florets before blending to preserve textural contrast. Cooking the spaghetti directly in the soup releases starch into the broth and creates a naturally creamier consistency.
t: Pasta with Romanesco broccoli belongs to Rome’s long tradition of vegetable-and-pasta minestra dishes, where inexpensive seasonal produce is stretched into a complete meal. Anchovy, garlic, chile, and tomato reflect the assertive pantry flavors typical of Roman home cooking.

Roman Pasta and Lentils

A lentil-and-mixed-pasta soup with carrot, celery, garlic, tomato, and potato.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

1 1/2 cups Italian lentils
2 1/2 cups mixed pasta
1 medium carrot
1 celery stalk
1 garlic clove
3 tbsp tomato sauce
2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
2 cups plus 2 tbsp vegetable broth
1 small potato

Preparation

1. Rinse the lentils thoroughly under cold water.

2. Finely chop the carrot, celery, and garlic.

3. Heat the olive oil in a medium pot.

4. Add the carrot, celery, and garlic and cook over medium heat for 5 minutes, stirring regularly.

5. Add the vegetable broth, tomato sauce, and lentils.

6. Peel the potato, cut it into 4 pieces, and add it to the pot.

7. Bring to a gentle boil, partially cover, and cook for 30 minutes.

8. Remove the potato pieces, mash them with a fork, and return them to the pot.

9. Add the mixed pasta.

10. Cook for 8–10 minutes, stirring often and checking the larger pasta shapes during the final 2 minutes.

11. Turn off the heat and rest for 5 minutes.

Serving

Divide among 4 bowls and serve hot.

Chef's Note

Mashed potato thickens the soup without flour or cream. Mixed pasta contains shapes with different cooking times, so checking the larger pieces during the final minutes keeps everything properly al dente.
t: Pasta and lentils is part of central Italy’s cucina povera tradition, built from inexpensive legumes, pasta, and aromatic vegetables. Roman household versions vary widely, but the essential idea remains the same: a thick, nourishing one-pot soup made creamy by starch rather than dairy.

Potato Gnocchi with Castrato Ragù

Homemade potato gnocchi with a slow-cooked castrato ragù of red wine, tomato, and herbs.

Yield: 6 servings

Ingredients

For the gnocchi
about 2 1/4 lb potatoes
2 cups type 00 flour
1 egg
1 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1/2 tsp fine salt

For the castrato ragù
about 1 1/2 lb castrato stew meat
1 celery stalk
1 small carrot
1 white onion
1 garlic clove
3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1 cup red wine
2 cups tomato sauce
1 bay leaf
2 sage leaves
1 rosemary sprig
1 whole clove
1 1/3 tsp fine salt
1/2 tsp ground black pepper

For cooking the gnocchi
5 1/4 qt water
2 tbsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Peel the potatoes and steam until completely tender, about 25–30 minutes.

2. Rice them while still hot and spread them on the work surface for 5 minutes.

3. Add the salt, egg, and olive oil.

4. Gradually incorporate the flour and knead briefly until soft and even.

5. Divide the dough into ropes about 3/4 inch thick, cut into 3/4-inch pieces, and ridge them on a gnocchi board.

6. For the sauce, finely chop the onion, celery, carrot, and garlic.

7. Heat the olive oil in a pot and cook the vegetables over low heat for 8 minutes.

8. Add the castrato and brown for 10 minutes, turning the pieces on all sides.

9. Add the red wine and cook for 5 minutes, until the sharp alcohol aroma has evaporated.

10. Add the tomato sauce, bay leaf, sage, rosemary, clove, salt, and pepper.

11. Cover with the lid slightly ajar and cook over low heat for 90 minutes, stirring every 15 minutes.

12. Bring the cooking water and salt to a boil.

13. Cook the gnocchi in 3–4 batches.

14. Lift them out with a slotted spoon as soon as they float and transfer directly to the sauce.

15. Stir gently over low heat for 1 minute.

Serving

Divide into 6 portions and serve immediately.

Chef's Note

Work the gnocchi dough only until the flour is incorporated; prolonged kneading develops gluten and makes the gnocchi rubbery. Cook the ragù slowly until the castrato is very tender.
t: Potato gnocchi with a slow castrato sauce reflects central Italy’s pastoral meat cookery, where mature sheep or wether meat is softened through long braising with wine, tomato, and herbs. The exact origin of this specific pairing is not firmly documented.

Pappardelle with Wild Boar

Egg pappardelle with a Tuscan wild-boar ragù of red wine, tomato, and aromatic herbs.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

about 3/4 lb egg pappardelle
about 2/3 lb wild boar
about 1/2 cup peeled tomatoes
1 medium onion
1 carrot
1 celery stalk
1 garlic clove
1/3 cup plus 1 tbsp red wine
2 bay leaves
2 sage leaves
1 rosemary sprig
3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1 tsp fine salt
1/2 tsp ground black pepper

For cooking the pasta
3 3/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1 tsp coarse salt

Preparation

1. Cut the wild boar into 3/8-inch cubes.

2. Finely chop the onion, carrot, celery, and garlic.

3. In a cold casserole, combine the olive oil, vegetables, wild boar, bay leaves, sage, and rosemary needles.

4. Place over high heat and brown for 10 minutes.

5. Add the red wine and cook until completely evaporated, about 4–5 minutes.

6. Add the chopped peeled tomatoes, salt, and pepper.

7. Cover and cook over very low heat for 60 minutes.

8. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil.

9. Cook the pappardelle al dente.

10. Drain and transfer directly to the ragù.

11. Toss over low heat for 1 minute.

Serving

Divide among 4 plates and serve hot.

Chef's Note

Use high heat during the initial browning to concentrate the wild-boar flavor. After adding the tomatoes, switch to a very gentle one-hour simmer so the meat becomes tender without drying out.
t: Wild-boar ragù is a classic expression of Tuscan game cooking, especially in wooded inland areas with strong hunting traditions. Long cooking with wine, herbs, and tomato tames the meat’s intensity, while broad egg pappardelle are traditionally suited to substantial ragùs.

Pappardelle with Hare Ragù

Pappardelle with hare marinated in red wine and slowly cooked with vegetables, tomato, sage, and bay leaf.

Yield: 6 servings

Ingredients

1 medium hare, cleaned and gutted
about 1 1/8 lb pappardelle
2 cups plus 2 tbsp red wine
1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil
1 onion
2 garlic cloves
1 carrot
1 celery stalk
2 bay leaves
2 sage leaves
3 cups plus 2 tbsp tomato passata
1/2 cup grated pecorino
1 1/3 tsp fine salt
1/2 tsp ground black pepper

For cooking the pasta
5 1/4 qt water
2 tbsp coarse salt

Preparation

1. Cut the hare into even pieces, rinse briefly, and dry thoroughly.

2. Place the meat in a bowl with the red wine, onion, garlic, carrot, celery, bay leaves, and sage.

3. Cover and refrigerate for at least 2 hours.

4. Drain the meat. Strain and reserve the wine. Cut the marinade vegetables into small pieces.

5. Heat the olive oil in a pot.

6. Brown the vegetables for 6 minutes.

7. Add the hare and brown on all sides for 10 minutes.

8. Add the strained wine and cook over low heat until completely evaporated, about 10 minutes.

9. Add the passata, salt, and pepper.

10. Cook over very low heat for 90 minutes with the lid slightly ajar.

11. Remove the hare pieces, strip the meat from the bones, and return it to the sauce.

12. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil.

13. Cook the pappardelle al dente and drain.

14. Dress with the hare ragù and 6 tbsp pecorino.

Serving

Divide among 6 plates and finish with the remaining 2 tbsp pecorino.

Chef's Note

The marinade seasons the game and builds the aromatic base of the ragù. Let the wine evaporate completely before adding tomato so the sauce does not retain a harsh wine flavor.
t: Hare ragù belongs to Tuscany’s longstanding game-cooking tradition, particularly in rural areas where hunting shaped autumn and winter tables. The meat is commonly marinated in wine and herbs before slow cooking, then paired with broad pappardelle. Its regional identity remains firmly rooted at the table today.

Pici with Aglione Tomato Sauce

Hand-rolled Tuscan pici with a sauce of Val di Chiana aglione garlic, tomato, and chile.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

For the pici
4 cups type 0 flour
1 cup plus 1 tbsp warm water
3/4 tsp fine salt
1 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1/3 cup remilled durum semolina for dusting

For the sauce
5 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
4 large aglione garlic cloves or fresh garlic cloves
1 red chile
about 2 cups tomato pulp
3/4 tsp fine salt

For cooking the pici
5 1/4 qt water
2 tbsp coarse salt

Preparation

1. Put the flour in a large bowl and add the fine salt.

2. Add the olive oil and gradually pour in the warm water while mixing with a fork.

3. Transfer the dough to the work surface and knead for 10 minutes until smooth.

4. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

5. For the sauce, heat the olive oil in a heavy-bottomed skillet.

6. Lightly crush the aglione cloves and add them with the chile.

7. Cook over low heat for 3 minutes without browning the garlic.

8. Add the tomato pulp and salt. Cook over low heat for 10 minutes.

9. Roll the dough to about 3/16 inch thick.

10. Cut into strips 3/8 inch wide and roll each strip on the work surface into a long picio.

11. Coat the pici lightly with semolina and arrange on a tray without overlapping.

12. Bring the cooking water and salt to a boil.

13. Cook the pici for about 5 minutes.

14. Drain al dente and transfer directly to the sauce.

15. Toss over medium heat for 1 minute.

Serving

Divide among 4 plates and serve immediately.

Chef's Note

Val di Chiana aglione has a sweeter, gentler flavor than ordinary garlic. Cooking it slowly without browning prevents bitterness and lets its aroma merge with the tomato.
t: Pici are a hand-rolled peasant pasta of southern Tuscany, especially Siena, Val d’Orcia, and Val di Chiana. Aglione is the large, mild garlic traditionally grown in Val di Chiana, making the tomato-and-garlic sauce one of the area’s defining pairings. Its place at the table endures.

Pici with Cinta Senese Ragù

Tuscan pici with a slow ragù of Cinta Senese pork loin and sausage, red wine, tomato, bay leaf, and juniper.

3/4 lb fresh pici
about 1 1/8 lb Cinta Senese pork loin

1. Finely chop the celery, carrots, and onion.

2. Heat the olive oil in a wide-bottomed pot with the bay leaves and crushed juniper berries.

3. Add the vegetables and brown for 8 minutes.

4. Cut the pork loin first into slices 3/16 inch thick, then into strips, and finally into small cubes.

6. Remove the sausage casing, break the meat into pieces, and add it to the pot.

12. Cook the pici al dente, drain, and transfer directly to the ragù.

13. Toss over medium heat for 1 minute.

Divide among 4 plates and serve very hot.

Before adding wine and tomato, let the liquid released by the meat evaporate completely. This concentrates the browning and allows the ragù to develop deeper flavor during the two-hour simmer.

Gnudi with Butter and Sage

Tuscan ricotta-and-spinach gnudi, lightly floured and served with butter, sage, and Parmigiano Reggiano.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

1 1/3 cups cooked spinach, drained and thoroughly squeezed
1 cup fresh ricotta, well drained
3 tbsp grated Parmigiano Reggiano
1 egg
1/3 cup type 00 flour for coating
4 tbsp unsalted butter
8 sage leaves
1/4 tsp freshly grated nutmeg
2/3 tsp fine salt
3 tbsp grated Parmigiano Reggiano for serving

For cooking the gnudi
3 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1/2 tsp coarse salt

Preparation

1. Place the ricotta in a colander and refrigerate for at least 4 hours to drain.

2. Squeeze the spinach until no more water comes out, then finely chop it.

3. Combine the ricotta, spinach, 3 tablespoons Parmigiano, and egg in a bowl.

4. Add the nutmeg and fine salt. Mix with a fork until even.

5. Spread the flour on a tray.

6. Shape the mixture into 20 balls slightly smaller than a walnut and roll them gently in the flour.

7. Bring the cooking water and salt to a boil.

8. Meanwhile, melt the butter in a skillet and add the sage leaves.

9. Cook the butter and sage over medium-low heat for 3 minutes, until the butter smells nutty without turning dark.

10. Cook the gnudi in 2 batches. Lift them out with a slotted spoon as soon as they rise to the surface.

11. Transfer directly to the butter and sage and roll gently for 30 seconds.

Serving

Divide among 4 plates and finish with the remaining 3 tablespoons Parmigiano Reggiano.

Chef's Note

The ricotta and spinach must be very dry. Excess moisture makes the mixture fragile and forces the use of more flour, while thorough draining keeps the gnudi tender but stable during boiling.
t: Known as gnudi in Florence and malfatti around Siena, these ‘naked’ ravioli are essentially the ricotta-and-spinach filling without its pasta wrapper. They belong to Tuscany’s frugal rural cooking, transforming simple dairy and greens into a delicate first course.

Tortelli Maremmani

Large Maremma-style tortelli filled with spinach and chard, sheep's-milk ricotta, eggs, Parmigiano, and nutmeg, finished with butter and sage.

Yield: 6 servings

Ingredients

For the pasta dough
4 cups type 0 or all-purpose flour
4 large eggs
2/3 tsp fine salt

For the filling
2 1/2 cups cooked spinach and chard, squeezed very dry and finely chopped
1 1/4 cups well-drained sheep's-milk ricotta
2 large eggs
4 tbsp finely grated Parmigiano Reggiano
1/4 tsp freshly grated nutmeg
3/4 tsp fine salt
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper

For finishing
4 tbsp butter
8 fresh sage leaves
2/3 cup finely grated Parmigiano Reggiano

For cooking the tortelli
6 1/3 qt water
2 tbsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Make the pasta dough. Mound the flour on the work surface. Beat the 4 eggs with the salt and pour them into the center.

2. Incorporate the flour with a fork, then knead by hand for 10–12 minutes, until smooth, elastic, and fairly firm.

3. Wrap the dough and rest for 30 minutes.

4. Wash the spinach and chard thoroughly. Put them in a pot while still wet from the final rinse, cover, and cook over medium heat for 5–7 minutes, until wilted.

5. Drain, cool, and squeeze the greens very dry. Chop finely with a knife.

6. Mix the greens, ricotta, 2 eggs, 4 tablespoons Parmigiano, nutmeg, salt, and pepper until uniform.

7. Roll the pasta thin, about 1/32 inch, and cut into even strips.

8. Place a heaping teaspoon of filling every 3 inches along one half of each strip.

9. Fold the pasta over the filling. Press around each mound to expel air and seal completely.

10. Cut the tortelli with a fluted wheel, leaving a broad border of pasta around the filling.

11. Arrange on a semolina-dusted tray and dry for 20 minutes.

12. Bring the cooking water and salt to a boil. Cook the tortelli in batches for at least 10 minutes, then lift them out gently with a slotted spoon.

13. Melt the butter in a wide skillet over low heat. Add the sage and cook for 2 minutes without browning the butter.

14. Layer the tortelli on a warm serving platter, seasoning each layer with sage butter and Parmigiano.

15. Rest for 2 minutes before serving.

Service

Abruzzese Sagne a Pèzze with Cicerchie

Abruzzese irregular semolina pasta with grass peas, tomato, garlic, rosemary, chile, parsley, and Pecorino.

Yield: 4 generous servings

Ingredients

For the grass peas
1 1/2 cups dried grass peas
8 1/2 cups water for soaking, changed twice
8 1/2 cups fresh water for cooking
2 bay leaves
1 whole unpeeled garlic clove
1 celery stalk, halved

For the sagne
1 7/8 cups fine durum-wheat semolina
3/4 cup warm water
1/2 tsp fine salt
2 tbsp semolina for dusting

For the sauce
1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil
3 garlic cloves, thinly sliced
1 fresh rosemary sprig
1 dried red chile
3/4 cup crushed peeled tomatoes
3/4 tsp fine salt
2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil for finishing
1 tbsp finely chopped fresh parsley
2 tbsp finely grated Abruzzese Pecorino
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper

For cooking the sagne
3 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Soak the grass peas in the cold water for 24 hours, replacing all of the water twice.

2. Drain and rinse. Transfer to a pot with the fresh water, bay leaves, whole garlic, and celery.

3. Bring to a gentle boil and cook for 90–120 minutes, until tender. Remove the bay, garlic, and celery and reserve the cooking broth.

4. Make the sagne. Combine the semolina and salt. Gradually add the warm water and knead for 10 minutes, until firm and smooth.

5. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

6. Roll the dough to about 1/16 inch thick and cut into irregular diamond shapes. Dust with the semolina.

7. Heat the olive oil in a wide saucepan. Add the sliced garlic, rosemary, and chile and cook over low heat for 2 minutes.

8. Add the tomatoes and cook for 6 minutes.

9. Add the cooked grass peas with about 2 cups plus 2 tablespoons of their cooking broth. Add the salt and simmer for 10 minutes.

10. Coarsely mash about one-quarter of the grass peas to thicken the broth naturally.

11. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil. Cook the sagne for 3 minutes.

12. Lift the sagne directly into the grass-pea mixture with a slotted spoon and finish cooking for 2–3 minutes, stirring continuously.

13. Turn off the heat and fold in the finishing olive oil.

14. Rest for 2 minutes.

Service

Divide among 4 soup bowls and finish with parsley, black pepper, and Abruzzese Pecorino.

Chef's note

Mashing only part of the grass peas creates creaminess while preserving the rustic texture of the legumes.

Maccheroni alla Mulinara

Hand-rolled Abruzzese macaroni with a long-cooked mixed-meat tomato ragù.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

For the macaroni
6 2/3 cups flour
1 cup plus 1 tbsp warm water
1 large egg
1 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
3/4 tsp fine salt

For the ragù
2/3 lb mixed ground pork and beef
4 1/4 cups tomato pulp
1/2 onion, finely chopped
2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1 tsp fine salt
1/4 tsp freshly grated nutmeg
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper

For cooking the pasta
6 1/3 qt water
2 tbsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Make the ragù. Heat the olive oil in a saucepan over medium-low heat.

2. Add the onion and cook for 5 minutes.

3. Add the ground meat and brown for 8 minutes, breaking it apart with a spoon.

4. Add the nutmeg, salt, pepper, and tomato pulp.

5. Bring to a gentle simmer, reduce the heat, and cook for at least 2 hours, stirring every 15–20 minutes, until thick.

6. Make the macaroni. Combine the flour and salt and form a well.

7. Add the egg, olive oil, and about 3/4 cup plus 1 tablespoon of the warm water to the center.

8. Knead for 10–12 minutes, gradually adding the remaining water until the dough is uniform, firm, but workable.

9. Seal the dough in a clean food-storage bag or wrap well and rest for 10 minutes.

10. Divide the dough into small rounds.

11. Work each piece between your hands and on the work surface until it becomes a long, even strand of macaroni.

12. Arrange the strands well separated on a lightly floured work surface.

13. Bring the cooking water and salt to a boil.

14. Cook the macaroni for 10–15 minutes, checking the texture after 10 minutes.

15. Drain and immediately dress with the ragù.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and serve very hot.

Chef's note

The dough should be firm enough to roll by hand without breaking, yet elastic enough to stretch into long strands.

Maccheroni con le Ceppe

Civitella del Tronto ceppe, hand-shaped around a thin metal rod and served with mixed-meat ragù and Pecorino.

Yield: 4 servings

For the ceppe
4 cups plus 2 tbsp flour
3 large eggs
1/3 cup plus 1 tbsp water
3 tbsp olive oil, plus a little for greasing
3/4 tsp fine salt

For the ragù
about 1/2 lb mixed ground beef and pork
2 cups plus 2 tbsp tomato passata
1/2 onion, finely chopped
1/2 carrot, finely chopped
1/2 celery stalk, finely chopped

3/4 tsp fine salt
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper
2/3 cup finely grated Abruzzese Pecorino

For cooking the pasta
5 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 2 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Make the ragù. Heat the olive oil in a saucepan over medium-low heat.

2. Add the onion, carrot, and celery and cook for 6 minutes.

3. Add the meat and brown for 7–8 minutes.

4. Pour in the red wine and cook for 3 minutes.

5. Add the passata, salt, and pepper. Cook over low heat for at least 90 minutes.

6. Make the ceppe. Mound the flour on the work surface and add the eggs, water, olive oil, and salt.

7. Knead for 10 minutes, until soft but not sticky.

8. Put the dough in a lightly greased bowl, cover, and rest for 30 minutes.

9. Divide the dough into small equal pieces.

10. Roll each piece to about 6 inches long.

11. Wrap each piece around a thin uncoated metal pasta rod.

12. Roll gently, then slide out the rod to create a hollow macaroni shape.

13. Arrange the ceppe on a floured cloth without overlapping.

14. Bring the cooking water and salt to a boil.

15. Cook the ceppe for 15–20 minutes, checking the texture after 15 minutes.

16. Drain and dress with the ragù.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and finish with the Abruzzese Pecorino.

Chef's note

The ceppe should have a clear hollow center so the ragù can enter the pasta instead of coating only the outside.

Teramo-style Scrippelle Timballo

Teramo layered timballo with thin scrippelle, tiny meatballs, meat sauce, mozzarella, Parmigiano, and a savory greens mixture.

Yield: 6 servings

Ingredients

For about 20 scrippelle
10 large eggs
3/4 cup plus 1 tbsp type 00 flour
2 1/2 cups water
3/4 tsp fine salt
2 tbsp oil for greasing the skillet

For the tiny meatballs
1 7/16 lb finely ground beef
1 large egg
2/3 cup finely grated Parmigiano Reggiano
1/4 tsp freshly grated nutmeg
1 tsp fine salt
1/2 cup oil for browning

For the meat sauce
1 1/8 lb meaty beef bones
1 large chicken leg
1 onion
1 carrot
2/3 cup dry white wine
2 cups plus 2 tbsp water
6 1/3 cups tomato passata
2 whole cloves
1/4 tsp freshly grated nutmeg
1 1/3 tsp fine salt
2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil

For the greens mixture
about 1 lb mixed field greens, chard, and spinach
2 tbsp butter
1 garlic clove
2/3 cup finely grated Parmigiano Reggiano
2 large eggs
2 cups plus 2 tbsp whole milk
3/4 tsp fine salt

For assembly
about 3/4 lb well-drained mozzarella, diced
1 1/2 cups finely grated Parmigiano Reggiano
2 tbsp butter for the dish and surface

Preparation

1. Make the scrippelle. Whisk the eggs, flour, and salt, then gradually add the water until the batter is very thin and smooth.

2. Heat a 9 1/2-inch nonstick skillet and grease it very lightly.

3. Pour in a small ladle of batter and immediately rotate the skillet to create a paper-thin layer.

4. Cook for about 30–45 seconds, turn, and cook the second side for another 15–30 seconds. Continue until you have about 20 scrippelle.

5. Make the tiny meatballs. Combine the beef, egg, Parmigiano, nutmeg, and salt.

6. Form meatballs about 3/8 inch in diameter.

7. Heat the oil in a skillet and brown the meatballs in batches for 2–3 minutes. Drain and reserve.

8. Make the sauce. Heat the olive oil in a large pot. Add the beef bones, chicken leg, onion, and carrot and brown for 10 minutes.

9. Pour in the wine and cook for 3 minutes.

10. Add the water, nutmeg, cloves, salt, and passata.

11. Cook over low heat for about 2 hours. Remove the bones, chicken, onion, carrot, and cloves.

12. Put the tiny meatballs into a generous ladle of sauce and simmer for 5 minutes.

13. Prepare the greens. Boil until tender, drain, and squeeze very dry.

14. Melt the butter in a skillet, add the garlic and greens, and sauté for 4 minutes. Remove the garlic.

15. Chop the greens finely and mix with the Parmigiano, eggs, milk, and salt.

16. Butter a deep 6-serving baking dish and line it with parchment.

17. Line the bottom and sides with scrippelle, allowing several to hang over the edges for closing.

18. Build layers of scrippelle, meatballs, sauce, mozzarella, Parmigiano, and greens mixture.

19. Continue until all ingredients are used, finishing with scrippelle. Fold the overhanging scrippelle over the top.

20. Dot the surface with the remaining butter.

21. Cover first with parchment and then with foil.

22. Bake in a preheated 480°F oven for about 60 minutes.

23. Rest for 15 minutes before unmolding or cutting.

Service

Cut into 6 portions and serve hot.

Chef's note

The scrippelle should be paper-thin because they function as the pasta layers of the timballo and should separate the fillings without making the dish heavy.

Scrippelle ’Mbusse

Paper-thin Teramo scrippelle rolled and served submerged in hot chicken or capon broth.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

For the scrippelle
4 large eggs
4 tbsp type 00 or all-purpose flour
1 cup plus 1 tbsp water
1 tbsp oil
1/3 tsp fine salt

For the broth
1 small chicken or capon, about 3 1/4 lb
1 onion, halved
1 carrot
1 celery stalk
8 1/2 cups cold water
1 1/3 tsp fine salt

For serving
3/4 cup finely grated Parmigiano Reggiano

Preparation

1. Make the broth. Put the chicken or capon, onion, carrot, celery, and cold water in a large pot.

2. Bring slowly to a boil, skimming away any foam that rises.

3. Reduce the heat and simmer for about 2 hours.

4. Add the salt during the final 20 minutes.

5. Remove the meat and vegetables and strain the broth carefully. Skim away excess fat and keep very hot.

6. Make the scrippelle. Whisk the eggs, flour, and salt until completely smooth.

7. Gradually whisk in all of the measured water until the batter is very fluid and completely smooth.

8. Heat a nonstick skillet and grease it very lightly with the oil.

9. Pour in a small ladle of batter and immediately rotate the skillet to form a paper-thin layer.

10. Cook for about 30 seconds, turn, and cook the second side for 15–20 seconds.

11. Continue until all of the batter is used.

12. Roll each scrippella tightly without tearing it.

Service

Arrange the rolled scrippelle in soup bowls, pour the boiling-hot broth over them, and finish with Parmigiano.

Chef's note

The batter should be much thinner than ordinary crêpe batter because a traditional scrippella is almost veil-thin.

Preparation

1. Soak the clams in the cold salted water for at least 4 hours, replacing the salted water twice. Rinse thoroughly.

2. Scrub and debeard the mussels.

3. Score the tomatoes, blanch for 1 minute, chill in cold water, peel, seed, and chop.

4. Put the clams and mussels in a wide pot, cover, and cook for about 5 minutes, removing them as they open. Discard any that remain closed.

5. Strain the shellfish liquid carefully. Remove about three-quarters of the shellfish from their shells, leaving the remainder in the shell.

6. Heat the olive oil in a large pan with the garlic and 1 tablespoon parsley for 1 minute.

7. Add the tomatoes and cook over high heat for 2 minutes.

8. Add the baby squid and cuttlefish. Pour in 1/2 cup strained shellfish liquid and cook for 15 minutes.

9. Add the langoustine tails, clams, mussels, salt, and chile. Cook over medium-low heat for another 10 minutes.

10. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil. Cook the linguine until al dente.

11. Drain and transfer to the seafood sauce.

12. Toss over medium heat for 1 minute.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and finish with the remaining parsley.

Chef's note

The strained clam-and-mussel liquid goes into the sauce because it concentrates the seafood flavor without requiring additional broth.

Foil-baked Linguine with Small Clams

Linguine with small clams, tomato, white wine, garlic, ginger, chile, and parsley, finished in a foil packet.

Yield: 3–4 servings

2 1/4 lb small clams
7/8 lb linguine
3 ripe tomatoes, diced
1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil
2 garlic cloves, sliced
1/4 tsp dried chile flakes
6 thin slices fresh ginger
1/3 cup plus 1 tbsp dry white wine

For purging the clams
2 1/8 qt cold water
3 tbsp plus 1 tsp coarse salt

For cooking the pasta
4 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1/3 tsp fine salt
3 tbsp pasta cooking water to reserve

Preparation

1. Soak the clams in the cold salted water for at least 2 hours. Drain and rinse.

2. Heat the olive oil in a large pan. Add the garlic, chile, ginger, fine salt, and half of the parsley.

3. Cook over medium-low heat for 2 minutes.

4. Add the clams, pour in the wine, and cover.

5. Increase the heat and cook for 4–5 minutes, shaking the pan, until the clams open. Discard any that remain closed.

6. Strain the liquid from the pan through a fine sieve and return it to the pan with the clams.

7. Preheat the oven to 350°F.

8. Line a large baking dish with two overlapping sheets of foil, leaving enough excess to seal the packet.

9. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil.

10. Cook the linguine for less than half of the package's stated cooking time. Reserve the pasta water.

11. Transfer the linguine to the pan with the clams and toss for 30 seconds.

12. Transfer everything to the foil packet. Add the tomatoes, remaining parsley, and reserved pasta water.

13. Seal the packet completely, leaving a little interior space for steam.

14. Bake at 350°F for 5–7 minutes.

Service

Open the packet carefully and divide immediately among 3–4 plates.

Chef's note

The pasta enters the oven very undercooked. Steam from the clams and tomatoes finishes it without making the linguine soft.

1/2 cup pasta cooking water to reserve

Preparation

1. Make the pasta. Mound the flour on the work surface and add the salt.

2. Gradually add the warm water and knead for 10 minutes, until firm and smooth.

3. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.

4. Heat the olive oil in a large heavy pot.

5. Add the garlic, onion, celery, carrot, and parsley and cook for 8 minutes.

6. Add the sausages, lamb ribs, veal, rooster, and pork ribs.

7. Brown for 12–15 minutes, turning the meats.

8. Pour in the Trebbiano and cook for 4 minutes.

9. Add the tomatoes, basil, bay leaf, rosemary, chile, and salt.

10. Cook over very low heat for at least 3 hours, adding hot water in 1/2-cup portions whenever the sauce reduces too far.

11. Remove all of the meat, bay leaf, and rosemary. Pass the sauce through a food mill or blend until uniform. Keep the meat warm for serving.

Sweet Ricotta Ravioli with Meat Ragù

Teramo-style half-moon ravioli filled with lightly sweetened ricotta and served with savory meat ragù.

Yield: 2 generous servings

Ingredients

For the pasta
1 2/3 cups type 00 flour
2/3 cup fine durum-wheat semolina
2 large eggs
1/4 cup hot water, added gradually
1/3 tsp fine salt

For the filling
3/4 cup plus 2 tbsp well-drained fresh ricotta
3 tbsp sugar

For the ragù
2/3 lb mixed ground beef and pork
1 2/3 cups tomato passata
1/2 onion, finely chopped
2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1/3 cup red wine
3/4 tsp fine salt
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper

For cooking the ravioli
3 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Make the ragù. Heat the olive oil in a saucepan over medium-low heat.

2. Add the onion and cook for 5 minutes.

3. Add the meat and brown for 8 minutes.

4. Pour in the wine and cook for 3 minutes.

5. Add the passata, salt, and pepper. Cook over low heat for at least 60 minutes.

6. Make the pasta. Combine the type 00 flour and semolina in a mound.

7. Add the eggs and salt to the center and begin incorporating the flours.

8. Knead for about 15 minutes, adding hot water 1 tablespoon at a time only if the dough is too firm.

9. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

10. Mix the ricotta and sugar until uniform.

11. Divide the dough and roll it into thin sheets, progressively reducing the pasta-machine setting.

12. Place teaspoonfuls of filling along one half of the pasta sheet.

13. Fold the pasta over, press out the air, and seal firmly around the filling.

14. Cut half-moon ravioli with a fluted wheel.

15. Arrange on a floured tray without overlapping.

16. Bring the cooking water and salt to a boil.

17. Cook the ravioli for 5–6 minutes.

18. Lift out with a slotted spoon and immediately dress with generous meat ragù.

Service

Divide between 2 plates and serve very hot.

Chef's note

The contrast between lightly sweetened ricotta and savory meat ragù is intentional. Careful sealing keeps the filling inside during boiling.

Cavatelli with Pork Ragù

Fresh cavatelli with slow-cooked pork, tomato, red wine, and Pecorino.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

1 1/3 lb fresh cavatelli
1 1/8 lb pork ribs or pork stew meat
3 cups tomato passata
1/2 white or yellow onion, finely chopped
3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1/3 cup plus 1 tbsp red wine
1 tsp fine salt
3/4 cup finely grated Pecorino

For cooking the cavatelli
5 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 2 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Heat the olive oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot.

2. Add the onion and cook gently for 5–6 minutes, until soft and just beginning to turn golden.

3. Add the pork and brown well on all sides for 8–10 minutes.

4. Pour in the red wine and cook for 3 minutes, until the sharp alcohol aroma has largely cooked away.

5. Add the passata and salt.

6. Bring to a gentle simmer, cover partially, and cook over very low heat for at least 2 hours, turning the meat every 20–30 minutes.

7. When the pork is tender and the sauce is thick, transfer the meat to a warm plate and keep covered.

8. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil.

9. Cook the fresh cavatelli for a few minutes, until they rise and are al dente.

10. Drain and immediately dress with generous pork ragù.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and finish with the Pecorino. Serve the pork alongside the pasta or as a second course.

Chef's note

The sauce needs a long, slow simmer so it thickens while the pork becomes tender enough to separate easily from the bone or cut with a fork.

Cavatelli alla Molisana

Molise-style cavatelli with slow pork-and-sausage ragù, tomato, red wine, and Pecorino.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

1 1/8 lb fresh cavatelli
1 7/16 lb mixed pork ribs and pork shoulder
2 fresh pork sausages
4 1/4 cups crushed peeled tomatoes
1 tbsp tomato paste
1 onion, thinly sliced
2 garlic cloves
3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1/2 cup dry red wine
1 tsp fine salt
3/4 cup finely grated Pecorino

For cooking the cavatelli
5 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 2 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Heat the olive oil in a wide heavy-bottomed pot.

2. Add the onion and garlic and cook over medium-low heat for 5–6 minutes, until lightly golden.

3. Add the pork and brown for 8 minutes, turning the pieces on all sides.

4. Remove the sausage casings, crumble the sausage, and add it to the pot. Cook for another 5 minutes.

5. Pour in the red wine and cook for 3 minutes, until the sharp alcohol aroma has largely cooked away.

6. Add the tomatoes, tomato paste, and salt.

7. Cover with the lid slightly ajar and cook over low heat for about 2 hours, stirring every 20 minutes.

8. When the pork is tender and the sauce is thick, transfer the larger pork pieces to a warm plate and keep covered.

9. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil.

10. Cook the fresh cavatelli until al dente.

11. Drain and transfer directly to the ragù. Toss over low heat for 1 minute.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and finish with the Pecorino. Serve the pork pieces separately or alongside the pasta.

Chef's note

Keep the ragù at a slow simmer so the pork and sausage season the tomato without reducing it too quickly.
